content: The study by Lopez et al. (2012) was downgraded due to the low quality of the intervention. In one study, 1% of participants indicated they would begin using contraception within the next six months, while another study reported 8% of participants planning to do so. In a 2008 trial, two intervention groups were compared. One group received four postnatal home visits, while the other received only one. The group with four visits had 52% of participants using contraception, whereas the group with one visit had 37% (107 out of 289 participants) using contraception. A 1998 study included structured baseline household questionnaires and one-on-one health education at birth and three months postpartum. However, neither the subjects nor the health educators were blinded, and there was a high loss to follow-up, with 25% lost at three months and 27% at six months. This study had three experimental groups and one control group. Group A received health education immediately after birth and at three months postpartum, Group B received education only at birth, and Group C received education only at three months. The control group (Group D) received no health education. The paper compared combined Groups A and B to combined Groups C and D but did not provide the number of participants assessed in each group, only the overall total. A 2003 study involved five structured postnatal home visits by nurse midwives. There was an unclear risk of performance and detection bias due to a lack of information on blinding. The study had a small sample size, with 139 enrolled and 124 assessed. A 2004 study included counseling, a videotape about oral contraceptives, and written materials. There was an unclear risk of performance and detection bias due to insufficient information on blinding. The study had a small sample size, with only 33 participants randomized, and 52% dropped out at one-year follow-up. The study reported the proportion of women still using oral contraceptives at one year, with some switching to other methods. However, the percentages were based on the total number of subjects rather than by group, as calculated by GRADE. A 1995 paper described issues around post-abortion care and recommendations for private and public abortion services but did not include any interventions, subjects, or results. Another paper from 1997 described post-abortion care in Nepal, reporting a high acceptance of family planning (70%) but did not specify the number of patients involved. A 2012 paper summarized the proportion of women receiving contraception before and after family planning services were strengthened across countries but did not provide sufficient detail to enter results into GRADE. A 2002 study included only women who wanted to postpone their next pregnancy for at least two years, suggesting potential for increased interest or use of family planning. However, for most outcomes, the number of events was less than 300, and no relative or absolute effects were provided in the paper. A 1999 study used three different family planning models, varying by who delivered the services and where they were delivered. The only results reported were the proportions of patients leaving the hospital with a contraceptive method: 82% for Model 1, 63% for Model 2, and 75% for Model 3. However, the number of patients in each model was not provided. A 2004 study assessed manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) services in Nepal, comparing them to abortion services offered in the main operating theater. While some counseling was provided, the study did not directly address post-abortion family planning counseling. The paper reported that 16% of MVA patients attended the six-week follow-up, but the disparity in numbers was unclear. A 2007 study in urban Tanzania reported that 95% of women left the hospital ward with a contraceptive method, while in rural Tanzania, 71% of women were provided with a contraceptive method. However, the observational nature of the study and lack of comparison to pre-counseling contraceptive use introduced a high risk of bias. A 2013 study on mobile outreach services for IUDs and implants noted that interviews were retrospective, introducing recall bias, and data was self-reported. A 2000 study on provider training stated that quality improvements could not be linked to outcome behaviors such as continued contraceptive use. The paper did not provide statistical results to support claims of significant increases. A 2007 study on the National Adolescent Friendly Clinic Initiative (NAFCI) in South Africa used a quality triangle approach, including defining, improving, and measuring quality. However, the study noted risks of selection bias, lack of statistical power due to a small number of clinics, and a lack of adolescent clients at some clinics. A 2005 study in India assessed local initiatives in three areas, reporting contraceptive use near or above 60% at the end of the programs. However, the paper did not provide the number of individuals contributing to these proportions or clarify how the reported 78% increase in contraceptive use was calculated.
